lost.value: Lost on arrival at Mars on Sept. 23, 1999. Ground software used English units while onboard software worked in metric; the error sent the spacecraft too close to Mars.

clues.title: Lopsided solar wing
clues.text: The solar array sat on one side of the craft. Sunlight pushed on it, so small thrusters fired far more often than the navigators expected to keep the craft steady.
clues.verdict: Real, and it made things worse: more firings meant the error grew faster. But each firing was logged. The bug was in how the pushes were written down.

evidence.value: Angular momentum desaturation (AMD) events happened 10-14 times more often than the navigation team expected, because MCO's solar array was asymmetrical.
evidence.source: MCO Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (Nov. 10, 1999), section 2 and Contributing Cause No. 1

clues.title: Thruster-firing file
clues.text: After every small thruster firing, the spacecraft team's software wrote down how hard the thrusters pushed, and sent the file to the navigators in another state.
clues.verdict: Found it! The file gave each push in pound-force seconds, but the navigators read the numbers as newton-seconds.

evidence.value: The SM_FORCES software was required to give its output in newton-seconds (N·s). Instead the data in the Angular Momentum Desaturation (AMD) file was in pound-force seconds (lbf·s).
evidence.source: MCO Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (Nov. 10, 1999), section 4: MCO Root Cause

clues.title: Skipped safety burn
clues.text: A last-chance course correction (TCM-5) was ready to raise the craft if it came in too low. It was discussed just before arrival, but never done.
clues.verdict: Real, and it might have saved the craft at the last minute. But it would only have patched the symptom: the bad data was still there.

evidence.value: A request to perform TCM-5 was discussed verbally shortly before the orbit insertion procedure began, but was never executed.
evidence.source: MCO Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (Nov. 10, 1999), Contributing Cause No. 3

clues.title: Busy navigators
clues.text: The navigation team was looking after three missions at the same time, so very few people were watching this one.
clues.verdict: Real, and it made the mistake harder to catch. But the navigators were working with numbers that were wrong from the start.

evidence.value: The operations project was running three missions at once (Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Climate Orbiter, Mars Polar Lander); MCO navigation was handled by the navigation team lead and the MCO navigator.
evidence.source: MCO Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report (Nov. 10, 1999), Contributing Cause No. 6
